body.text: In short:
Ecuadorian fishermen who allege they were maimed in a drone attack and kidnapped by US forces are suing the Trump administration.
They claim they are victims of a war crime orchestrated by the US military while on a Galapagos Islands fishing trip.
What's next?
Lawyers say the fishermen want at least $US5 million ($7.4m) in damages.
Hundreds of kilometres at sea off Ecuador, 16 fishermen allege they became victims of a war crime orchestrated by the Trump administration.
In a lawsuit filed in the US on Monday, local time, the group claimed they were maimed in a drone bombing, captured and tortured by US forces and taken as prisoners to El Salvador.
They are seeking at least $US5 million ($7.4m) in damages after suffering what their lawyers describe as "severe psychological trauma … physical pain, scarring and disability".
Galapagos trip became 'fiery torture'
Court documents filed in Pennsylvania show that on March 2, the 16 men set sail from the port city of Manta, west of the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.
Aboard the La Negra Francesca Duarte II, the group was bound for the World Heritage-protected Galapagos Islands for a two-week fishing trip, lawyer Daniel Kovalik said in the documents.

A day after departing, the US Southern Command, which oversees the Trump administration's Latin American and Caribbean military activities, announced a joint mission with Ecuador to combat drug trafficking.

During the group's return voyage a fortnight later, they were intercepted by the Ecuadorian Navy and their boat was inspected for three hours before they were cleared of any wrongdoing and set free, the documents show.
On March 17, the fishermen allege their vessel was attacked by two aerial drones launched from a ship operated by US forces, in a stretch of sea between San Cristóbal Island and Manta.
The group claims the bombing engulfed their boat in flames, set at least two crew members alight, including one whose leg skin was burned to the bone, and sunk the vessel.

Mr Kovalik said the fishermen escaped into the ocean and onto smaller boats towed by their main vessel, only to be surveilled by another airborne drone and aimed at by sailors with long rifles on a nearby ship.
"All of these sailors spoke English. Some of them wore military camouflage uniforms marked by US flags, while others wore life vests which contained the words 'US Coast Guard',"
the documents said.

The group's lawyers said one crew member, Jordy Alexander Flores Lucas, was offered medical treatment after being taken aboard the US vessel, but alleges the other men were handled in "cruel and inhumane ways amounting to torture".

They allege the fishermen's hands were zip-tied, their heads covered by plastic hoods, they were given only 500 millilitres of water and no food, and were forced to stand barefoot on the vessel's hot iron deck.
Mr Flores Lucas also alleged a military officer using a translator claimed his crew were responsible for the attack and laughed about the fishing boat's sinking.
The US military has previously claimed responsibility for strikes it launched against so-called "narco-terrorists" and often shares videos of the attacks.
It has not claimed responsibility for the attack on the La Negra Francesca Duarte II.

On March 18, the fishermen were moved as prisoners to a Salvadoran ship that sailed for a week to a port in El Salvador where they were held "in a comprehensive care centre for foreign immigrants", the documents show.
Two of the crew members' injuries were so serious they were hospitalised, before the entire group was flown home by the end of March, according to the lawsuit.
The documents say the men remain in "dire economic straits" after their boat's sinking and continue to suffer psychological trauma.
Mr Flores Lucas and another crew member, Leonel Alberto Pilay Barahona, also continue to live with "severe physical pain, scarring and disability".
Trump's 'unlawful drug war' condemned again
Since September last year, the US military has launched strikes on more than 70 vessels in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, killing at least 235 people.
Donald Trump says the operation, known as Southern Spear, is necessary because the US is in an armed conflict with Latin American drug gangs transporting deadly drugs to America.
The strikes began amid an escalation in tensions that culminated in the "capture" of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro by US forces in a covert nighttime military operation.
In September, UN Human Rights Council Special Rapporteur Ben Saul found the strikes could be considered crimes against humanity, violating international, maritime and humanitarian law.
In his court filing, Mr Kovalik echoed that sentiment.
"These premeditated and intentional attacks against defenceless people lack any plausible legal justification," he said.
"None of the plaintiffs were members of, or affiliated with, drug cartels or any other designated terrorist group."
In a statement to the ABC, the White House said US President Donald Trump would look to continue the strikes.

"President Trump promised to take on the cartels — and he has taken unprecedented action to stop the scourge of narco-terrorism that has resulted in the needless deaths of innocent Americans," White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly said.
"The President will continue to use every element of American power to stop drugs from flooding into our country and to bring those responsible to justice."

From late August to mid-September, the US military said it intercepted and sank at least eight Ecuadorian vessels accused of being used as resupply points for drug traffickers working with the criminal gang Los Choneros.
The vessels collectively had about 160 crew members. Of these, 56 were released without charge by court order and 40 were acquitted for lack of evidence.
Another 50 are awaiting trial and 14 were not formally charged, Human Rights Watch said in a statement.
Hernan Flores, the captain of the La Negra Francesca Duarte II, told Reuters his crew felt a lawsuit was their final resort for compensation.
"The boat was all we had. Nobody in Ecuador is helping us … They did all that damage to us, and by the grace of God, we're alive," he said.
ABC/Reuters
